content: 1. Assessment and Management of Tears or Episiotomies: Examine the tear to determine its severity: A small tear involving only the vaginal mucosa, connective tissues, and underlying muscles is classified as a firstor second-degree tear. If there is no bleeding, the wound can be left open. A long and deep tear extending through the perineum and involving the anal sphincter and rectal mucosa is classified as a thirdor fourth-degree tear. Cover the wound with a clean pad and urgently refer the patient to a hospital. Suture the tear using sterile equipment, universal precautions, and aseptic techniques. Use local infiltration with lidocaine and absorbable polyglycol suture material. Provide emotional support to the patient. Do not suture if more than 12 hours have passed since delivery. 2. Management of a Distended Bladder: Encourage the woman to urinate. If she is unable to do so, catheterize the bladder using clean gloves, antiseptic cleaning of the urethral area, and proper sterile technique. 3. Emergency Treatment for Severe Pre-eclampsia and Eclampsia: Administer magnesium sulfate as a loading dose: Insert an IV line and administer fluids slowly (e.g., 1 liter of normal saline or Ringer’s lactate over 6–8 hours). Give 4 g of magnesium sulfate (20 mL of a 20% solution) intravenously over 20 minutes. Additionally, administer 10 g intramuscularly (5 g in each buttock with 1 mL of 2% lignocaine in the same syringe). If convulsions recur, administer an additional 2 g of magnesium sulfate intravenously over 20 minutes. If convulsions persist, administer diazepam. Monitor the patient’s urine output, respiratory rate, and knee-jerk reflexes before giving the next dose of magnesium sulfate. Do not administer further doses if the knee jerk is absent, urine output is less than 100 mL in 4 hours, or respiratory rate is below 16 breaths per minute. If respiratory depression occurs after magnesium sulfate administration, stop the medication and administer calcium gluconate (1 g IV over 10 minutes). 4. Management of Convulsions in Early Pregnancy or Magnesium Sulfate Toxicity: Administer diazepam as a loading dose (10 mg IV slowly over 2 minutes). If convulsions recur, repeat the dose. For maintenance, administer 40 mg of diazepam in 500 mL of IV fluids over 6–8 hours, ensuring the patient remains sedated but rousable. Do not exceed 100 mg in 24 hours. 5. Management of Hypertension in Pre-eclampsia: If IV administration is not possible, give the medication intramuscularly. 6. Management of Infections: Administer appropriate IV or IM antibiotics before referral. If referral is delayed or not possible, continue antibiotics for 48 hours after the patient becomes fever-free. If symptoms persist or the patient becomes weak or experiences abdominal pain postpartum, urgently refer her to a hospital. 7. Management of Malaria in Pregnancy: In the first trimester, treat uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria with quinine and clindamycin for 7 days. Administer oral quinine and clindamycin once the patient can tolerate oral medications. In the second and third trimesters, administer artesunate (4 mg/kg IM or IV at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then once daily) until oral artesunate can be given to complete a 7-day course. 8. Referral Protocols: After emergency management, discuss the decision with the patient and her family. Organize transportation and financial aid if needed. Inform the referral center and accompany the patient if possible. 9. Management of Bleeding in Early Pregnancy and Post-abortion Care: Assess the patient’s history, symptoms, and physical signs to classify the condition: For complicated abortion (e.g., foul-smelling discharge, abdominal pain, or fever), insert an IV line, administer fluids, provide pain relief, and give appropriate antibiotics before urgent referral. For threatened abortion with light bleeding, observe for 4–6 hours. If bleeding decreases, allow the patient to go home with instructions to return if bleeding increases. Follow up in 2 days. For complete abortion, provide self-care advice, family planning counseling, and instructions to return if bleeding persists beyond 2 days. For ectopic pregnancy (e.g., abdominal pain, fainting, or pallor), insert an IV line, administer fluids, and urgently refer to a hospital. 10. Post-abortion Care: Advise rest, hygiene (e.g., changing pads every 4–6 hours), and avoiding sexual activity until bleeding stops. Counsel on danger signs such as increased bleeding, foul-smelling discharge, abdominal pain, fever, or dizziness. Provide family planning counseling, emphasizing that pregnancy can occur soon after an abortion if contraception is not used. Any method can be initiated immediately after an uncomplicated first-trimester abortion. 11. Antenatal Care: During each antenatal visit, assess the pregnancy status, check for danger signs, and develop a birth and emergency plan. Screen for pre-eclampsia, anemia, syphilis, and HIV. Record all findings and treatments in the patient’s records.
